# Code, Test, and Deploy on One Machine with NVIDIA RTX Spark

 Bring coding agents, model customization, and CUDA-accelerated development to your everyday PC 

 Oct 16, 2026 

 By Annamalai Chockalingam 

 AI-Generated Summary 

- NVIDIA RTX Spark combines the GB10 system-on-a-chip with up to 128GB of unified memory to let developers run local coding agents, test, and deploy on a single PC.
- The platform delivers 4.6x faster coding-agent performance, 2.7x faster fine-tuning, and 1.8x faster code compilation compared with Intel Panther Lake 12Xe.
- NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to expand the Windows on Arm software stack, adding the first PyTorch-CUDA build, Python 3.15 native by default, over 2,000 Conda packages, and Arm-compatible versions for more than 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages.
- Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74B-parameter mixture-of-experts model quantized to 2 bits, is purpose-built for local agents on RTX Spark and runs on llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, and LM Studio.
- Decision models now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth enable agents to choose actions up to 200x faster than traditional reasoning loops.
- NVIDIA AI for Media SDKs with video super resolution, frame generation, and TrueHDR are available on RTX Spark via PyPI and NGC.

...

AI agents are changing how software gets built. Developers have gone from writing every line of code by hand to directing agents that write most of the code. As a result, the current workflow is split across a laptop, a cloud model API, and a cloud VM. 

NVIDIA RTX Spark is built for AI development. Thanks to the NVIDIA GB10 system-on-a-chip and large unified memory, developers can run local coding agents, access AI frameworks, and code, test, and deploy on a single PC.

...

## One machine to code, test, and deploy

RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops enable developers to complete all of their workflow on a single machine.

Developers can choose to work in Windows, including the new Windows Developer Config, developed with Microsoft, which installs the top development frameworks, mutes notifications, enhances the terminal, and can move their task bar to the side. Or they can work in Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they get access to the same environment and dependencies they will use when deploying to the cloud. This enables developers to complete all their work in their target OS without code migrations. And since RTX Spark has an NVIDIA GPU, developers can test and deploy to the largest local AI installed base: 150 million RTX PCs, as well as virtually all the clouds in the world that run on NVIDIA GPUs.

With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI compute, developers can run coding models locally, including Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, reducing cloud coding agent token consumption.

...

## The performance you need for AI development 

Development has gone from being a CPU-bound workload, where performance was determined mostly by the CPU, to a GPU-bound workload. AI developers today need to run inference to run their coding agents and test their apps; for fine-tuning and training models; and yes, still a bit of compilation.

Thanks to the NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU in RTX Spark, these laptops and desktops come equipped with all the compute required for inference, fine-tuning and compilation. Compared with Intel’s Panther Lake 12Xe, RTX Spark delivers 4.6x performance on coding agents, 2.7x performance on fine-tuning, and 1.8x performance on code compilation.

...

### New Nemotron models offer more options for local agents

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. 

This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.

Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. 

Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source, including training data, weights and recipes, so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.

signals.title: Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0 | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0

October 16, 2026 11 min read

Table of Contents

TL;DR: Reflection's Beam is a 501B-parameter MoE with 23B active parameters per token. vLLM supports it from day 0 and optimizes it on NVIDIA Blackwell:

- Full feature support. Reasoning, tool calling, and structured outputs work out of the box, and you can run the model with tensor, data, or expert parallelism.
- Agent-driven optimization. Coding agents optimized the model autonomously, making batch-1 decode 2.71× faster and prefill 1.87× faster than our first implementation.
- DFlash2 with adaptive verification. With Beam's DFlash2 drafter, a single request reaches 708 tokens/s on TP8, with an acceptance length of 3.7. Adaptive verification, which decides each step how many draft tokens are worth verifying, adds 10% more throughput at high concurrency.

To try it, use our Docker image `vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam`:

Copy code

```
docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam \
  reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
  -tp 4 \
  --max-num-seqs 128 \
  --reasoning-parser beam \
  --tool-call-parser beam --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER"}' \
  --kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false}' \
  --speculative-config '{
    "method": "dflash",
    "model": "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2",
    "num_speculative_tokens": 7,
    "attention_backend": "FLASH_ATTN"
  }'
```

...

## Model architecture

Beam is a 52-layer MoE decoder with hidden size 5120. The MoE routing follows DeepSeek-V3. The main differences are in the attention layers and in how the residual stream is normalized.

Figure 1: Beam's layer stack and one sparse decoder layer. Gold marks the parts that differ from a standard pre-norm MoE. Open it full-screen.

...

### Attention

- Hybrid sliding-window and NoPE layers. 43 layers use sliding-window attention over the last 512 tokens, with RoPE. The other 9 (every sixth layer, plus the last) attend over the full context with no positional encoding (NoPE).
- SSMax on NoPE layers. Without RoPE, attention flattens as the number of keys grows. SSMax scales each query by `(1 + p/2048)^0.1`, where `p` is the 1-based position, so the softmax sharpens as the context grows.
- GQA with per-head Q/K norm. 48 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128. Q and K are RMS-normalized per head before RoPE or SSMax.
- Sigmoid output gate. Before `o_proj`, each head's output is multiplied by σ(gate + bias), where the gate comes from its own full-width projection with a learned per-head bias. A head can be turned down or off token by token.
- Small KV cache. Only the 9 full-attention layers keep KV for the whole sequence: 

- 9 × 2 × 8 × 128 values per token, or 36 KiB in BF16 and 18 KiB in FP8.
- About 18 GiB of FP8 KV for a full 1M-token context, before sharding.

...

## Agent-driven optimization

Our initial version of implementation was an unoptimized, almost pure PyTorch version of the model. We then optimized it autonomously with coding agents: they profiled the model, wrote the kernels, and benchmarked each change. On TP8, the seven changes below brought batch-1 decode from 8.95 ms to 3.30 ms per step, and an 8 × 2K prefill from 328 ms to 176 ms.

...

After these changes, one MoE layer runs as 13 kernels in batch-1 decode on TP8.

Figure 3: Kernels in launch order for one MoE layer, from a rank-0 trace of batch-1 TP8 decode. Gold kernels were written, fused, or extended for Beam. Each kernel lists the operations it computes. Open it full-screen.

- 6 kernels were written, fused, or extended for Beam. Every small Beam-specific op is merged into a neighbor, and both all-reduces live inside norm kernels.
- 7 kernels come from libraries: TRTLLM-gen attention, the cuBLAS output projection, and the TRTLLM NVFP4 MoE path (quantization, two routing kernels, two grouped GEMMs). Most of the remaining time is here, so they are next.

...

## Attention DP + MegaMoE

Figure 4: FlashInfer CuteDSL NVFP4 MegaMoE can fuse the communications with expert computation.

In the high concurrency region, Beam's performance can be further improved by combining Attention DP with MegaMoE, powered by FlashInfer's CuTe DSL NVFP4 MegaMoE kernel. The Finalize + norm

...

## DFlash2 speculative decoding

Beam ships with a DFlash2 draft head, which vLLM supports from day 0. Instead of drafting one token at a time, it predicts a whole block of tokens in a single forward pass from the target model's hidden states.

- Drafter. 5 sliding-window layers that read hidden states from 5 target layers and share the target's embedding and LM head. A grouped convolution and a small candidate selector restore some of the left-to-right dependency a parallel drafter loses.
- Adaptive verification. With `"enable_adaptive_verification": true`, vLLM predicts how likely each draft token is to be accepted and verifies only the ones worth their cost, instead of a fixed number per step. DFlash2 has no confidence head, so the acceptance estimate comes from the drafter's own logits (see our recent post on adaptive verification).
- Kernels. The drafter's convolution, norms, and KV writes are fused, and the whole draft step runs in a CUDA graph. FP8 KV cache works for the drafter too, with no change in acceptance.

Serving results on TP8, with and without adaptive verification, on the low-entropy category of SPEED-Bench's `throughput_1k` split: ~1K-token prompts, mostly code completion and text sorting, with greedy decoding and up to 4K output tokens. Low-entropy text is easier to predict, so expect lower acceptance on open-ended chat.

| Concurrency | Fixed draft (tok/s) | Adaptive (tok/s) | Change | Acceptance length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 708 | 707 | −0.1% | 3.71 → 3.61 |
| 8 | 3,232 | 3,221 | −0.3% | 3.67 → 3.57 |
| 32 | 7,744 | 8,275 | +6.9% | 3.68 → 3.29 |
| 128 | 15,012 | 16,632 | +10.8% | 3.68 → 3.23 |

Adaptive verification pays off under load. At concurrency 128 it raises output throughput by 10.8% and cuts p99 TPOT by 9%, while verifying fewer draft tokens per step, which lowers acceptance length slightly but saves more compute than it loses. At low concurrency, where extra draft tokens are nearly free, it is neutral.

...

## AgentX benchmark

Figure 5: Beam 1.0 NVFP4 AgentX benchmark showing up to 88K total tok/s per GPU and up to 350 tok/s per user on GB300.

We also tested Beam on AgentX, which replays multi-turn coding conversations to measure serving performance. With DFlash2, vLLM reached approximately 88K total tokens/s per GPU at 96 concurrent requests. Total throughput counts input and output tokens, including cached input. Input-token cache hit rates ranged from 91.4% to 95.6% across the sweep.

AgentX benchmark configuration: Beam 1.0 NVFP4 on 4× GB300 with TP4/EP1 and FP8 KV cache for both target and drafter. DFlash2 uses real acceptance (average AL 3.6 across measured points), block size 8, and probabilistic sampling. AgentX uses trajectory ratios 0.55–0.75, maximum reasoning effort, temperature 1.0, and 20 minutes per point. Total throughput includes cached input tokens. Source commits: vLLM 8e0922.

signals.title: ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars
signals.excerpt:
# ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars

OpenViking from ByteDance's Volcengine treats agent memory, knowledge and skills as a virtual filesystem, crossing 40,000 GitHub stars.

 By Marcello Babbili · AI-assisted newsroom October 19, 2026 3 min read 

Image generated by OpenAI

ByteDance's Volcengine team published OpenViking, an open-source context database that treats everything an AI agent knows as files under a `viking://` filesystem, and the project crossed 40,000 stars on GitHub this week after gaining 105 stars in a single day on the platform's trending list S¹.

The approach challenges how most agent builders work today: stitching together separate systems for retrieval-augmented generation (the standard method for feeding documents into a model), conversation memory, and tool or skill management. OpenViking collapses all three into one virtual filesystem that an agent can browse and read on demand P² P⁴.

...

My read: This is the first agent-memory project I've seen that refuses to separate knowledge from memory from skills at the storage layer. Most teams I watch are still gluing a vector database to a chat-history buffer and calling it done. The filesystem metaphor is elegant, but the benchmark numbers are entirely self-reported and nobody outside the Volcengine team has verified them. I'd want to see independent tau2-bench results before believing the performance claims, and the 40,000-star count tells me about GitHub momentum, not production readiness.

...

### One filesystem, three context types

The Viking team, part of ByteDance's cloud infrastructure arm Volcengine, organises context into three types: resources for reference material, memories for information retained from interactions, and skills for task procedures P⁴. Each piece of context loads in three tiers: L0, a one-sentence abstract; L1, a core overview; and L2, the full original data S¹. An agent scans the L0 summaries to decide what it needs, then drills down to L2 only for relevant items, which keeps token consumption down.

When a conversation session ends, OpenViking commits and archives it as Markdown files that a developer can read and edit by hand S¹. Memories sit in readable text, not a binary store, which makes debugging and correction straightforward.

...

### The benchmarks nobody has checked

The project reports evaluation results on two benchmarks: LoCoMo, which tests long-conversation user memory, and tau2-bench, which tests multi-turn agent tasks S¹. Version 0.3.22 used Doubao 2.0 Pro, Volcengine's own vision-language model, for the memory evaluation S¹. These results are self-reported. The repository does not include peer-reviewed or third-party-audited benchmark data, and the README is the maintainers' description of their own work, not an independent review.

A developer who wants to try the system without committing to an install can use OpenViking Studio, a browser-based demo that requires no setup S¹.

The repository is written primarily in Python and carries the volcengine organisation label on GitHub, though the about page confirms the team sits inside ByteDance's Volcengine unit P².

Until an independent team reproduces the LoCoMo or tau2-bench results, the 40,000-star count measures interest, not proof.

signals.title: AWS Introduces Strands Decider 2B and Strands Box for AI Agent Development - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
2B and Str ... Box ... AI Agent Development 

Oct 16, 2026 3 min read 

by

- Daniel Dominguez 

AWS has introduced two open-source projects for AI agent development: Strands Decider 2B, a small model designed to make decisions within agent workflows, and Strands Box, a sandbox for controlling agent execution. Both projects address different aspects of building agents that use tools, execute code, and interact with external systems.

Strands Decider 2B is a two-billion-parameter model designed to select between predefined options rather than generate lengthy text responses. It supports tasks such as model routing, tool selection, classification, guardrails, and context management. Instead of asking a general-purpose language model to generate an answer, developers can provide a set of choices and receive a decision with confidence scores.

The model is based on Qwen3.5-2B, with its language-model head replaced by a pointer head that scores candidate answers. It uses a rank-16 LoRA adapter for fine-tuning. AWS has released the model weights, training data, and scripts, allowing developers to run and modify the model locally.

According to AWS, Strands Decider 2B achieved a median decision latency of approximately 115 milliseconds on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 and 153 milliseconds for small tasks on an Apple M3 MacBook. The company also evaluated the model using JevBench, reporting 72.3% accuracy across 231 public tasks for its v19 checkpoint. Developers can install the strands-decider package and use its command-line interface or integrate the model into Strands agents.

...

The second project, Strands Box, is available in developer preview and provides an isolated environment for executing AI agents. It combines operating-system-level isolation with Dogwood, an open-source policy language that defines which actions an agent can perform. The sandbox supports shell commands, Python execution, MCP tools, filesystem operations, and network access.

Strands Box uses kernel-enforced isolation to route agent interactions through a policy layer. Developers can allow or deny actions based on their content and execution history. For example, a policy can require an agent to pass tests before pushing code to a repository or restrict the frequency of external API calls. These controls operate outside the language model, reducing reliance on prompt instructions to enforce execution boundaries.

AWS says Strands Box can work with different models and agent frameworks, whether running locally or in cloud environments. This allows developers to introduce execution policies without replacing their existing agent architecture.

...

Strands Decider 2B competes with TypeSafe AI's Jev, another specialized model designed to make structured decisions without generating lengthy responses. Both support classification, routing, and tool selection, returning confidence scores alongside their decisions. The main difference is deployment: Strands Decider 2B is open source and can run locally, while Jev is available through a managed API. AWS evaluated Strands Decider using JevBench, although the published results do not establish a direct performance advantage over Jev.

...

Strands Box addresses problems also handled by container-based sandboxes, Firecracker microVMs, and hosted agent execution environments. While conventional sandboxing primarily restricts filesystem, process, and network access, Strands Box adds policies based on tool arguments and previous actions. This allows developers to define conditions that must be satisfied before an agent executes specific operations.

...

Early developer feedback has focused on the practical limitations of integrating small decision models into agent workflows. In a hands-on tutorial, AWS Community Builder Yuuki Yamashita reported that:

> Strands Decider 2B could prevent an agent from making an unsupported weather-tool call.

GitHub discussions have also identified issues involving concurrent requests, Apple Silicon compatibility, and cold-start latency, highlighting areas developers may need to evaluate before using the model in production.

signals.excerpt:
Reflection has released Beam, their first model launch | Artificial Analysis

October 16, 2026

# Reflection’s first model, Beam, scores 30 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it #2 among US open weights models

Beam is an open weights model with 501B total and 23B active parameters

Key takeaways:

➤ Second among US open weights models: Beam scores 30, behind only Meta's Muse Spark Open (39) and ahead of yesterday’s NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (26) release. Outside China, only Muse Spark Open and the UAE's K2 Horizon (31) score higher

➤ Token efficient for its intelligence: Beam uses ~26k output tokens per Intelligence Index task compared to K2 Horizon, one point ahead, which uses twice as many (~52k). Proprietary models still set the frontier, with GPT-6 Astra (max) scoring 53 on the same budget (~27k)

➤ Strong on agentic workflows, weaker in the terminal: Beam scores 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA, 11 percentage points ahead of K2 Horizon (37.2%) and level with Qwen3.8 27B (48.2%). Terminal-Bench 4.0 is a weak point, where Beam scores 3.0%, behind Qwen3.8 27B (5.6%) and Muse Spark Open (8.1%)

➤ Knows more, guesses more: On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% of questions correctly, well ahead of K2 Horizon (18%) and Qwen3.8 27B (16%). But its hallucination rate is 47%, against 26% for K2 Horizon and 30% for Qwen3.8 27B, giving Beam a net index score of 1.5, ahead of both peers (−3.0 and −10.0)

Other model details

- Context window: 1M tokens
- Modalities: Text
- Parameters: 501B / 23B

Compared to open weights peers

Beam scores highly against US open weights models, trailing Meta's Muse Spark Open (39) and ahead of NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (26), all released this week. Among all open weights models it ranks tenth, one point behind K2 Horizon (31)

...

Highly token efficient

Beam uses ~26k output tokens per Intelligence Index task: ~19k for reasoning and ~7k for answers. Only 26% of its output goes to final answers, the 28th-lowest share of 219 models tested on Intelligence Index v4.3

Coding skills

Running in Mirror, Reflection's open-source CLI harness, Beam scores 28 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. It sits 15 points behind the next setup, Claude Code with Qwen3.8 Max (43), and 40 behind the leaders (68). It is, however, frugal: only Codex with GPT-6 Astra and Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol use fewer tokens

Intelligence Index Components

Across the ten evaluations in the Intelligence Index, Beam stands out on AutomationBench-AA (48.5%) and CritPt (13.1%), where it more than doubles K2 Horizon (4.6%) and Qwen3.8 27B (5.4%). Its weakest results are on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (3.0%) and AA-Briefcase (976 Elo)

signals.title: RoLaQ, MLA 모델 KV 캐시를 2비트로 줄여 KV 캐시 용량 3.96배 확보 | LUCAS AI News
signals.excerpt:
RoLaQ, MLA 모델 KV 캐시를 2비트로 줄여 KV 캐시 용량 3.96배 확보 | LUCAS AI News

# RoLaQ, MLA 모델 KV 캐시를 2비트로 줄여 KV 캐시 용량 3.96배 확보

MLA 구조 모델의 KV 캐시를 2비트로 저장하는 양자화 기법 RoLaQ가 arXiv에 공개됐다. DeepSeek-V2-Lite에서 BF16 대비 3.96배 용량과 2.51배 디코딩 처리량을 냈다고 연구진이 밝혔다.

루카스 · 2026년 10월 17일 00:36

멀티헤드 잠재 어텐션(MLA) 모델의 KV 캐시를 2비트로 저장하는 사후 보정 기법 RoLaQ(Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization)가 논문으로 공개됐다. 연구진은 DeepSeek-V2-Lite에서 같은 메모리 예산으로 BF16 KV 캐시의 3.96배 용량을 확보했다고 밝혔다. 입력 토큰이 256K일 때 디코딩 처리량은 BF16의 2.51배로, SGLang 구현으로 측정했다고 한다.

MLA는 토큰마다 키·값 캐시의 내용을 공유 잠재 표현 하나로 압축하는 어텐션 방식이다. 연구진은 이 구조가 긴 문맥 추론에서 낮은 비트로 저장하기에 알맞다고 설명했다. 다만 2비트에서는 이 표현의 오차가 어텐션 매칭과 값 읽기에 함께 영향을 주고, 그 영향은 오차의 방향과 복원 크기에 따라 달라진다고 했다.

...

## 회전과 범위를 함께 보정하는 방식

RoLaQ는 오프라인에서 회전과 범위를 함께 보정한다. 고정된 키·값 투영이 정의하는 부분공간 안에서 공유 회전을 다듬고, 양자화 범위를 함께 학습한다. 이때 임계값과 복원 이득을 묶어서, 공유 신호가 받는 영향을 제어한다.

보정에는 예측 일치와 어텐션 출력 지도가 쓰이며, 모델 가중치는 고정한 채로 진행한다. 모델을 다시 학습하지 않는 방식이다.

...

## 측정 결과

연구진은 MLA 모델 3종과 벤치마크 6개에서 비교한 2비트 방식 가운데 평균 정확도가 가장 높았다고 밝혔다. 토큰 보호를 쓰지 않은 경우와 쓴 경우 모두 해당한다.

signals.title: Beam Turns Frontier-Scale Openness Into an Infrastructure Decision · Hugging Face Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Beam Turns Frontier-Scale Openness Into an Infrastructure Decision

Reflection's 501B-parameter Beam model pairs sparse expert routing with a one-million-token context window, but its real test is whether teams can turn open weights into an operable, measurable system.

Hugging Face Blog Editorial Editorial team · 6 min read

Announcement: October 16, 2026 Published: October 17, 2026

Source artwork · Hugging Face / credited contributors ↗

THE SHORT VERSION

Beam offers unusual scale and control, but successful adoption depends on testing the complete serving and agent system—not merely loading the checkpoint.

Reflection has released Beam, a text model aimed at coding and agentic workloads, under Apache 2.0. Its headline scale is 501 billion parameters, while sparse mixture-of-experts routing activates about 23 billion parameters for each token. The release also advertises a one-million-token context window and provides BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints. Support spans Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, alongside a separate Rust-based serving harness.

Those specifications make Beam interesting, but they do not make deployment simple. Sparse activation reduces arithmetic per token; it does not make the inactive experts disappear from memory. For engineering teams, the useful question is therefore not whether Beam behaves like a 23B model or a 501B model. It behaves like each in a different part of the system, and capacity planning has to respect both.

...

## An evaluation path before committing hardware

The release offers several serving routes, which makes staged evaluation possible. Begin with a hosted endpoint to test prompt formats, response parsing, and task quality. This stage should use a frozen test set with explicit pass criteria, including refusal and recovery cases.

Next, compare checkpoint precision on representative tasks. Quantization should be evaluated against application outcomes, not only generic benchmarks. Track structured-output validity, tool-selection accuracy, long-context retrieval, latency percentiles, and cost per successful task. Small aggregate benchmark differences can conceal a material regression in one critical workflow.

Only then should a team reproduce the expected concurrency and context distribution on the intended hardware. Include cold starts, burst traffic, and degraded-node scenarios. This sequence keeps the biggest infrastructure decision until there is evidence that Beam solves the actual problem.

# Footnote: Agentic RAG with Sentence-Level Citations
An AI research agent for your documents. It decides what to search for, searches again when the results are thin, and every claim in its answer links to the exact sentence it came from.
The usual 'chat with your documents' build searches once with the user's words and hopes. A two-part question gets one search and half an answer. footnote replaces that fixed pipeline with an agent that works like a researcher, built around one rule: an answer you cannot check is not an answer.
## How it was built
Claude is given two tools, `search\_handbook` and `read\_page`, and loops until it can answer. Search results come back as sentence-level blocks, so every citation is validated by the API rather than typed by the model. Retrieval is a hand-written BM25 plus local bge-small vectors, merged with weighted reciprocal rank fusion and tuned on a 59-question eval set. The demo corpus is the public-domain 18F staff handbook, 232 pages.
## What it does
**Plans its own research.** A two-part question gets two searches, worded the way the handbook words things. Each step shows live in a side panel.
**Sentence-level citations.** Click a citation chip and the source passage scrolls into view with the exact sentence highlighted.
**Says when it doesn't know.** If nothing relevant turns up after retrying, it says the documents don't cover it instead of guessing.
**Swappable search.** Run the agent on hybrid, keyword-only or vector-only search, with each passage's rank in both shown.
## Stack
Python with FastAPI and a one-file HTML UI, Claude through the Anthropic SDK with no framework, and a CLI that prints each tool call. The screenshots come from a keyless demo mode where the model's turns are scripted and the searches and citations run for real.
Retrieval is the easy half. The hard half is making every sentence of the answer checkable.
Source code: github.com/IbrarYunus/footnote. More of my work: ibraryunus.com.

Startup Reflection AI Inc. today made the weights of Beam, its first large language model, available on Hugging Face.

# AI & Compute roundup: Hugging Face runs Meta’s 816B open model at 18 tokens a second on one 512GB Mac

Hugging Face ran Meta's 816B Muse Spark Open at 2-bit on one 512GB M3 Ultra Mac. Reflection's 501B Beam needs about 280 GB at 4-bit, and NVIDIA's Bolt 74B-A9B is built to fit 24GB.

October 19, 2026 · AI & Compute · 3 minute read · Saeid Yazdani

Two frontier-scale open-weight models landed a day apart, and both are mixture-of-experts designs: memory follows the total parameter count, while speed follows the few parameters active for each token. The second memory bill, the cache that grows with context, is where the two differ by roughly a factor of seven.

### Meta’s Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters and runs on a 512GB Mac at 2-bit

Muse Spark Open has about 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion of them active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens, according to Hugging Face’s launch post for the model. It takes text, images, audio and video and writes text. All 256 experts in each layer stay in memory while eight run per token, which puts the BF16 checkpoint at about 1.5 TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint is the 4-bit option for Blackwell GPUs: the post runs it on a single B200 node in transformers and on four GB300 GPUs in the SGLang reference setup, and its Inference Endpoints recipe uses eight RTX Pro 6000 cards with a context length of 131072 tokens.

The numbers a home lab can use come from Apple hardware. On an M3 Ultra with 512GB, an imatrix-calibrated 2-bit llama.cpp quantization uses 304 GB and generates 18 tokens a second. An oMLX 3-bit quantization takes about 344 GB and generates 21 tokens a second after a 1024-token prompt, with prompt processing at 225 tokens a second.

Context is where that Mac runs out of room. The post puts the BF16 cache at about 250 KB per token, or about 266 GB for a full million-token window. Added to the 304 GB of 2-bit weights, one full-length sequence would need about 570 GB, which is more than the machine has unless the cache is quantized too. That sum is our arithmetic from the post’s figures.

...

### Reflection’s Beam is a 501B Apache 2.0 model that needs about 280 GB at 4-bit

Beam is the first model from Reflection, a new US lab, and Hugging Face’s post describes it as a text-only model for coding and agent workflows with 501 billion parameters, 23 billion active per token, a one-million-token window and an Apache 2.0 license. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB. NVFP4 shrinks it to roughly 280 GB but needs Blackwell, so FP8 checkpoints cover Hopper and Ampere cards. Two B200s with 180 GB each can hold the weights and little else, so the post recommends four, with a full 8xB200 node, two B300s at 288 GB each or 8xRTX Pro 6000 as alternatives.

The cache is the smaller bill here. Only 9 of Beam’s 52 layers attend to the whole sequence, and the other 43 keep a 512-token sliding window, so the cache grows by about 36 KiB per token and reaches 36.08 GiB at one million tokens in BF16. That is roughly a seventh of Muse Spark Open’s 266 GB. Each layer caches the same 2,048 values per token in both models, so the gap comes from Muse Spark Open keeping 62 full-length layers against Beam’s 9.

Reflection’s benchmark table, reproduced in the post, shows little cost from quantization. SWEBench Verified reads 81.6% in BF16, 80.2% in FP8 and 80.7% in NVFP4. Terminal Bench v2.1 reads 80.1%, 78.9% and 78.2%.

Artificial Analysis, October 15, 2026: Vera Rubin NVL72 serves up to ~5.7x GB300 NVL72's throughput per MW.

By Elena Marsh 5 min read

Artificial Analysis published the first AA-AgentPerf results for NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 on October 15, 2026. In its Vera Rubin NVL72 benchmark, the rack serves up to about 5.7 times the total throughput per megawatt of the GB300 NVL72 it replaces on DeepSeek V4 Pro, about 5.4 times on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, about 3.0 times on GLM-5.2 and about 2.8 times on Kimi K3. Vera Rubin NVL72 is NVIDIA’s rack-scale system of the Rubin generation, with 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs in one NVLink domain. What NVIDIA has announced about the platform is collected in our Nvidia Rubin explainer, and the chip sits alongside its predecessors in our AI chips table.

...

## What AA-AgentPerf measures

AA-AgentPerf is a hardware benchmark built around coding agents rather than chat. According to Artificial Analysis’s methodology, it replays real coding-agent trajectories, produced by agents resolving issues in public code repositories, at a range of concurrency levels. Each simulated agent works through three trajectories in sequence and pauses after each reply for a tool-call time taken from real tool-call durations.

That traffic looks different from fixed-length prompts. Requests carry up to 132K input tokens, replies are often a short tool call, and on average 97% of a request’s input tokens repeat the previous request. Artificial Analysis says this makes KV cache capacity and reuse, uneven prefill and time to first token decisive. Our KV cache explainer covers why a repeated prefix can be served from cache instead of being processed again.

The headline metric is total throughput (input and output tokens, about 96% of them cached input) per megawatt of measured GPU power, plotted against per-user output speed at the 25th percentile. Measured power covers each GPU and its HBM as reported by NVIDIA’s telemetry, and excludes CPUs, networking and cooling.

signals.title: Georgia Tech, Nvidia, Stanford Boost LLM Inference Throughput — Die Signal
signals.excerpt:
# Georgia Tech, Nvidia, Stanford Boost LLM Inference via Memory

Georgia Tech, Nvidia and Stanford let GPUs read HBM and host DRAM at the same time, raising LLM inference throughput on existing accelerators.

3nm

Operator

Amara Osei

## Spec summary

1. S01 Georgia Tech, Nvidia and Stanford jointly published the research.
2. S02 The method improves LLM inference throughput by accessing HBM and host memory concurrently.
3. S03 It targets models whose weights and key-value caches exceed a single GPU's HBM capacity.
4. S04 Nvidia's participation links the work to its H100, H200 and B200 accelerator lines.
5. S05 The approach treats host DRAM as a working memory tier instead of an overflow store.

...

Researchers at Georgia Tech, Nvidia and Stanford have published a method that raises large language model inference throughput by letting accelerators access high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and host DRAM concurrently, rather than treating host memory as an overflow tier used only when HBM fills up.

The work targets a structural bottleneck in LLM deployment. Model weights and key-value caches have outgrown the HBM capacity of single accelerators, which forces operators to shard models across GPUs or offload tensors to host memory in sequential, blocking transfers. Both paths cost time.

...

## What does the technique change?

The paper's core move is scheduling. Instead of staging data from host DRAM into HBM before the compute units can touch it, the system overlaps reads from both pools during inference.

That shifts host memory from a fallback store into a working tier. The GPU draws on PCIe- or CXL-attached DRAM while it continues to stream from HBM, so the compute engines stall less often waiting for a transfer to finish.

The practical consequence: models that exceed local HBM can run on fewer accelerators, or serve more requests per second on the same hardware.

...

Three institutions appear on the work: Georgia Tech, Stanford and Nvidia. Nvidia's involvement signals vendor interest, since the company sells the HBM-equipped GPUs — H100 with 80 GB, H200 with 141 GB, B200 above that — whose capacity limits the technique addresses.

Capacity pressure keeps rising. Frontier-class LLMs now reach hundreds of gigabytes of weights, and key-value caches grow with context length and concurrent users. Memory, not floating-point throughput, increasingly sets the serving ceiling.

## Summary

Millions of machine learning models run locally on Arm devices, from edge devices to physical AI systems. It provides a layer-by-layer view of AI models, from large language models (LLMs) to neural graphics models, showing how they change during deployment to runtimes optimized for Arm.

Arm has contributed three open-source adapters, which make it easier for developers to explore Arm-relevant model formats and compilation flows directly in Model Explorer.

Now available on GitHub, these adapters add support for the following formats:

- TOSA (Tensor Operator Set Architecture) for Arm CPUs and Arm Ethos-U.
- VGF that enables visualization of VGF files from Arm ML SDK for Vulkan® for neural graphics and GPU workloads, and can be used with the Arm Neural Accelerator.
- PTE ExecuTorch files that enables visualization of PTE files for Arm Ethos-U NPU Backend, Arm® VGF Backend and XNNPACK targets.
- ExecuTorch adapter extension, a combined extension package that visualizes `.etrecord` graph files and overlays runtime profiling data from `.etdp` or `.etdump` files onto ETRecord graphs.

...

Developers need to understand whether a model can be fully delegated to their target backend or whether some operations still run on the CPU. A real-world use case of extracting the maximum performance from the accelerator is real-time object detection. It demands low-latency vision processing close to the sensor, often within tight power and memory constraints.

We converted the Ultralytics YOLO model to TOSA format for the Arm Ethos-U85 NPU.

Figure 4: The same Ultralytics model, with its NPU graph.

A preview integration between Arm ML Inference Advisor (MLIA) and Model Explorer is now available in VS Code, with a public release planned for the future.

MLIA checks compatibility with supported Arm targets and provides performance estimates or profiling results, with advice to guide optimization. # AMD adds day-0 support for Meta's Muse Spark Open

AMD said its Instinct MI350X and MI355X GPUs support Meta's Muse Spark Open on ROCm and vLLM, with BF16, MXFP4 and FP8 variants.

 Iris Coleman Oct 16, 2026 19:22 UTC 

 

AMD said on Thursday it has added day-0 support for Meta's Muse Spark Open on Instinct MI350X and MI355X GPUs using ROCm software and vLLM, positioning the stack for a large open-weight model aimed at coding and long-running reasoning tasks.

## Evidence and context

In the technical article published Oct. 15, 2026, AMD described Muse Spark Open as the first open-weight model in the Muse Spark family and said it is a natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 816 billion total parameters, 42 billion active per token and a 1 million-token context window. AMD said the model includes configurable reasoning and native tool calling, and that it is available on Hugging Face, Muse Code, the Meta Model API and OpenRouter.

AMD said the model can run on a single node of eight Instinct MI350X or MI355X GPUs, with 288 GB of HBM3E per GPU and 8 TB/s memory bandwidth, using tensor parallelism across eight GPUs. The company said the software stack is ROCm 7.2 with vLLM, along with the AMD AITER kernel library for attention, MoE and communication, and CUDA-graph capture for the decode step.

The article listed three supported checkpoints for vLLM: a BF16 open release, an MXFP4 AMD Quark export and an FP8 AMD Quark export using PTPC. AMD said the BF16 checkpoint can also be served with an opt-in mode that rounds routed experts to MXFP4 at load time, giving the MXFP4 memory and throughput profile without a separate checkpoint.

AMD also published performance figures from its tests. It said decode-step optimizations increased the MXFP4 checkpoint from 206 to 350 output tokens per second at four concurrent requests and from 719 to 1,180 at 32 concurrent requests. The company said expert parallelism added 7% to 20% throughput at 32 to 128 concurrent requests on MXFP4 and reduced time to first token by about 24%, reaching 2,197 tokens per second at 128. AMD said its tuned AITER fused-MoE table raised single-request decode throughput from 98 to 114 tokens per second on TP8, while DSpark speculative decoding reached 199 tokens per second in a single stream.

AMD said GSM8K accuracy stayed within a 94.4% to 95.5% range across its MXFP4 configurations. The company recommended different serving setups depending on load, including TP8 plus EP8 plus DSpark for up to about 64 concurrent requests and TP8 plus EP8 for higher loads. AMD also said the day-0 recipe is available in vLLM-recipe and that its ROCm vLLM Docker image is vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:muse-spark-open.

The article did not provide commercial terms for the support, and the reported throughput and latency figures were AMD's own test results on the configurations it described.

Baseten said Reflection trained Beam to solve coding and agentic tasks while using fewer tokens, with longer reinforcement learning rollouts letting the model practice multi-step problems and a length penalty applied during training to discourage unnecessary tokens. Users can adjust Beam’s reasoning effort parameter: lower settings favor shorter responses, while higher settings allow more reasoning on demanding tasks.

...

## Mirror CLI and Customization

Reflection also open-sourced Mirror CLI, a terminal agent harness trained alongside Beam. Mirror pairs a Python frontend covering prompts, skills, and developer tooling with a Rust agent core that drives the model, and it supports resumable conversations, parallel agents in separate worktrees, project instructions, MCP connections, and Python extensions. Reflection said it initially built Mirror for internal engineering use, with isolated workspaces, background sessions, and integrations into Slack, Linear, and GitHub, before evolving it into a tool it could open source.

Beam has been tested with Pi from Earendil, OpenCode from Anomaly, and Hermes from Nous Research across coding and knowledge-work tasks, including reading repositories, editing files, and running commands.
